one_liner: Size-capped append-only Swift log file (optional ring-buffer eviction); appends far faster than per-row-committed SQLite inserts.
what_it_does: CacheAdvance<T: Codable> persists a stream of log messages to one pre-created file with a fixed byte budget. Once the budget is reached it either rejects new messages or overwrites the oldest (ring buffer). The whole public API is init(fileURL:maximumBytes:shouldOverwriteOldMessages:decoder:encoder:), append(message:), messages() (read everything into an array), isEmpty() and isWritable(). There are no keys, queries, deletes or counts, so it replaces a hand-rolled 'SQLite table of log rows', not SQLite in general.
how_it_is_fast: Each append JSON-encodes the message (encoder is pluggable), prefixes it with a big-endian UInt32 length and writes it at the current FileHandle offset. It then rewrites one 8-byte offset field in a fixed 64-byte file header; an overwriting cache also updates the oldest-message pointer and advances a read cursor. That is a few write/seek syscalls per message. There is no SQL parsing, B-tree, journal, transaction or fsync (the source never calls synchronize/fsync). The SQLite path it is compared against pays a full autocommit transaction per insert.
when_to_use: Swift apps on iOS 15+/macOS 11+/tvOS/watchOS/visionOS (or Linux with Swift 6) that need a crash-surviving on-disk buffer of recent log or analytics events before upload
Write-heavy, read-rarely workloads: many small appends (tests use about 480 strings of roughly 50 bytes), then one bulk messages() read at upload or crash-report time
When you want a hard on-disk size cap with automatic eviction of the oldest entries (shouldOverwriteOldMessages: true) and no compaction or vacuum
When pulling in SQLite/Core Data just for a log table is overkill and a single dependency-free Swift source package is preferred
when_not_to_use: You need power-loss durability: appends are plain write() calls with no fsync, and the README only promises that data is 'persisted to disk' when append returns (i.e. handed to the OS)

You need keyed lookup, filtering, deleting specific entries, a message count or partial reads: messages() decodes the whole cache into memory, and there is no count API (proposed in issue #34, absent from the current source)
Read-heavy use: the author's own PR #41 reports that SQLite is 'significantly faster at reading messages'; reads cost two small read calls plus a JSON decode per message
Multi-threaded or multi-process writers: instances are not thread-safe, the class is not Sendable under Swift 6, and there is no file locking

Large messages or caches whose size or overwrite policy may change later: messages must stay under 2 GB, and changing maximumBytes or the overwrite flag after first use makes the file unwritable (fileNotWritable)

integration.dependencies: none (Foundation only); SQLite3 is imported only by the test target
integration.min_toolchain: Swift 6.0 tools / Swift 6 language mode (Xcode 16+); Objective-C support removed in 4.0.0
integration.platforms: iOS 15, tvOS 15, watchOS 7, macOS 11, Mac Catalyst 15, visionOS 1 (podspec); Linux x86-64 tested in CI with Swift 6.0.3 and 6.1; other OSes not documented
integration.thread_safety: Not thread-safe: use one instance from a single serial queue (README). Calls do synchronous disk I/O, so keep them off the main queue. No cross-process locking.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it replaces the pattern of a bounded SQLite log table (append plus read-all) behind a different, SQL-free Swift API; it does not replace SQLite for anything that needs queries, keys, transactions or durability guarantees

gotchas: The file must already exist (for example via FileManager.createFile) before init; the handles open with forUpdating/forWritingTo and fail otherwise. The README's sample uses a 'file:' argument label, but the real initializer takes 'fileURL:'.

maximumBytes and the overwrite flag are stored in the header and must never change: a mismatch leaves the file readable but append throws fileNotWritable. The encoder/decoder are not recorded, so changing them silently breaks decoding of old messages.

Crash windows are documented in the source: a crash between the data write and the header update loses the newest message, and a crash mid-write can yield CacheAdvanceError.fileCorrupted, after which the README says to delete the file.
The per-append cost is dominated by JSONEncoder (the author in PR #41 put encoding at about 15x the header cost); supply a cheaper MessageEncoder if throughput matters.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Every sibling here is a keyed store with point lookups (for example CalicoDB, also benchmarked against SQLite, NuDB or the RocksDB-derived engines) and mostly C/C++/Go. Pick CacheAdvance only when you are in Swift and need a bounded, append-then-dump log file rather than a key-value store; for any keyed or read-heavy workload a sibling (or SQLite itself) is the right tool.
verified_claims_summary: The '30x faster than SQLite' tagline is a first-party README claim from April 2020 with no published numbers, hardware or Xcode/Swift version. The PR that added the benchmarks (#41) said 'more than 15x' as a lower bound and mentioned runs above 50x; two days later the README was changed to 30x. The benchmarks are XCTest measure{} tests appending about 480 JSON-encoded Lorem-ipsum strings. The SQLite side runs COUNT(*), prepares a fresh INSERT and autocommits every row under default rollback-journal synchronous=FULL (per sqlite.org, a few dozen transactions per second versus 50,000+ plain INSERTs), while CacheAdvance never fsyncs. It therefore compares durable per-row transactions with page-cache writes, and a batched or WAL-mode SQLite baseline was never tested.
status_note: Active single-maintainer project (v4.0.0 June 2025, last push June 2026, 0 open issues, CI on Apple platforms and Linux); Apache-2.0 and 14 small Swift source files, so easy to vendor, though usage is modest (51 stars).
